vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent RequestID Validation in createMultipleDeploymentRequest Allows Duplicate Deployment Requests
vulnerabilities.description: The createMultipleDeploymentRequest function generates a unique requestID for each deployment in the array but only sets projects[projectId].requestDeploymentID to the last projectDeploymentId generated. This means that if the first deployment in the array has a valid requestID, but subsequent ones fail or are skipped, the project's requestDeploymentID still points to the last one, leaving earlier deployments unlinked and potentially reusable. This allows an attacker to submit multiple deployment requests with the same projectId and base64Proposal but different indices, and then call createDeploymentRequest with the first requestID to claim a deployment that was already partially processed, leading to double-spending of deployment slots.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection in createDeploymentRequest and createPrivateDeploymentRequest Allows Forced Execution Without Minimum Output Guarantees
vulnerabilities.description: The createDeploymentRequest and createPrivateDeploymentRequest functions allow users to trigger deployment requests without any mechanism to specify minimum acceptable outcomes (e.g., minimum worker reputation, minimum service quality, or rejection thresholds). An attacker can flood the system with low-quality deployment requests, forcing legitimate users to accept suboptimal workers or have their deployments assigned to malicious actors. Since there is no user-controlled bound on worker selection or solver reputation thresholds, users cannot protect themselves from unfavorable execution outcomes, violating Pattern 1.

vulnerabilities.title: Validation After State Change in submitDeploymentRequest Enables Invalid State Transitions
vulnerabilities.description: In submitDeploymentRequest, the function first sets requestDeploymentStatus[requestID].status = Status.Pickup and requestDeploymentStatus[requestID].deployWorkerAddr = msg.sender, then validates that the status was not already Pickup or GeneratedProof. This violates Pattern 2: validation occurs after state mutation. An attacker can call submitDeploymentRequest with a requestID that has already been picked or proven, and the state will be overwritten before the revert. This allows an attacker to steal a deployment assignment from a legitimate worker by submitting a transaction with higher gas, causing the original worker to lose their assignment and the attacker to claim it.

vulnerabilities.title: Reputation System Division by totalProposalRequest Can Round to Zero, Leading to Reputation Stagnation
vulnerabilities.description: In the setReputation function, when totalProposalRequest > 1000, the reputation increase is calculated as (reputation - 6 * factor) / totalProposalRequest. If reputation is only slightly above 6 * factor and totalProposalRequest is large (e.g., 10^6), the division rounds down to zero. This causes reputation to stop increasing entirely for high-volume solvers, effectively freezing their reputation. For example: if factor = 100, reputation = 601, totalProposalRequest = 10000, then (601 - 600) / 10000 = 0.0001 → 0. Reputation remains at 601 forever. This breaks the incentive mechanism and allows attackers to exploit reputation stagnation to dominate the system with low-effort solvers.

vulnerabilities.title: Signature Replay Vulnerability in createProposalRequestWithSig and createDeploymentRequestWithSig
vulnerabilities.description: The signature-based functions (createProposalRequestWithSig, createDeploymentRequestWithSig) use EIP712 but do not include a nonce or timestamp in the digest. The digest is computed as keccak256(abi.encodePacked(projectId, base64RecParam, serverURL)) — which is static for the same inputs. An attacker can capture a valid signature from a user and replay it indefinitely to create multiple proposal or deployment requests on behalf of the user. Since there is no replay protection (e.g., requestID or nonce in digest), the signature is reusable, enabling theft of user actions.

vulnerabilities.title: Partial Execution in createMultipleDeploymentRequest Leaves State Inconsistent
vulnerabilities.description: The createMultipleDeploymentRequest function loops through an array of base64Proposals and calls deploymentRequest for each. If one deploymentRequest reverts (e.g., due to invalid base64Proposal), the entire transaction reverts, but the totalDeploymentRequest counter has already been incremented by the number of successful iterations before the revert. This creates an accounting inconsistency: totalDeploymentRequest increases even though the deployment requests were not fully committed. This breaks protocol invariants and allows attackers to inflate totalDeploymentRequest without creating valid deployments, potentially manipulating reward distributions or fee calculations downstream.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Access to setWorkerPublicKey Allows Address Poisoning
vulnerabilities.description: The setWorkerPublicKey function allows any address to register a public key without any authorization or uniqueness check. An attacker can call setWorkerPublicKey with the address of a legitimate worker and a fake public key, causing the workerAddresses array to contain duplicate or poisoned entries. This breaks the integrity of the worker list and can cause downstream functions (e.g., getWorkerAddresses) to return corrupted data. Since there is no check for existing keys or access control, this enables denial-of-service and data manipulation attacks.
